# Private benchmark binary producer

This isolated `build.yml` builds one fixed validator revision and the fixed workload tools in a digest-pinned Ubuntu 22.04 container on Depot. It does not run a validator, use STS/MinIO, or read/write the benchmark binary cache. A successful private artifact contains only `tempo`, `txgen-tempo`, `bench`, `cpu-check`, and `manifest.json`.

The validator uses the locked profiling profile, no default features, and `asm-keccak,jemalloc,keccak-cache-global`. Both tools use their locked release profile and default features. Rust 1.98.1 is checked against its full commit, host, release date, and LLVM identity before building; its rustfmt component is installed for bindgen. All three binaries use explicit x86-64-v3 code generation and the fixed C/C++ flag `-DNO_PCLMUL`. The latter selects RocksDB's existing CRC fallback: its compatibility header otherwise infers PCLMUL from AVX, although v3 does not require it. The baseline CPU checker remains unchanged; this is a different build contract from historical host-native binaries and requires a separately labeled comparison.

The closed manifest binds the producer commit/run/attempt, workflow and helper hashes, exact source trees and Cargo files, dependency pins, compiler identities, flags, binary sizes/hashes, registration symbol/call verification, and ELF loader/library/version requirements. The OS image is pinned by its linux/amd64 manifest digest; installed distribution packages are not promised byte reproducible. Their actual compiler binaries and the resulting executable requirements are recorded. Consumer ABI and CPU admission remains mandatory; a successful producer build does not establish compatibility with any benchmark runner.

`rustflags`, `cflags`, and `cxxflags` describe code-generation flags. The separate `owned_source_build_toolchain_v1` policy adds Rust `--remap-path-prefix` and C/C++ `-ffile-prefix-map` mappings for the workspace, selected source, private temporary Cargo/build directories, and Rust toolchain to `/workspace`, `/source`, `/build`, and `/toolchain`. This removes those roots from compiler-generated debug/file paths; it is not a claim that arbitrary dependency data cannot embed other paths. Binary transport stays private.

`reject_host_native_v1` installs task-private compiler wrappers as `CC`/`CXX`. Before executing the fixed GCC/G++ paths, they reject response files, host-native/foreign `-march` or `-mtune` selections, and `-mcpu` overrides. Source-selected per-file ISA variants used by runtime-dispatched crypto remain allowed. This is an invocation guard, not a sandbox against hostile build scripts; exact immutable sources and locks remain part of the trust boundary. No inherited compiler wrappers, Cargo overrides, credentials, or native flags are passed to Cargo.

The CPU checker is compiled separately as static baseline x86-64 and checks CPUID plus OSXSAVE/XGETBV on every CPU in its inherited affinity, restoring that affinity afterward. It emits only schema/supported/checked/total. Consumers must check all intended validator and workload affinities are covered and independently validate dynamic-library symbol versions before using a v3 binary.

Each source group builds in its own fresh Cargo/target directory and is removed after its binaries are copied and checked. Source identity is checked before and after builds. Failed checks prevent artifact upload. Cargo has a per-invocation timeout and the job has a 90-minute timeout; this is not an end-to-end process-tree cleanup guarantee. No fallback compilation or cache lookup is part of the consumer protocol.

Relevant local validation: `python3 -m unittest discover -s .github/scripts -p test_bench_prebuilt_producer.py`. The tests include actual static CPU-check compilation, each required CPUID feature's rejection, compiler-wrapper execution, clean source/commit checks, closed manifest and ABI mutations, and fixed workflow/build commands. They do not substitute for an actual Depot build or consumer admission.

Failure diagnostics are a closed numeric JSON record in the private workflow log. `stage` identifies setup (1–5), validator build/source recheck (10–11), tool build/source recheck (20–21), binary hash/copy/ABI (12–14), registration verification (30), manifest construction/validation (31–32), final identity recheck (33), or publication (34). `role` is 0 unspecified, 1 Tempo, 2 txgen-tempo, 3 bench. `bytes` is the last hashed object's observed byte count; `clean` is 0 unchecked, 1 clean, 2 dirty. `abi` is 0 not started, 1 ELF header, 2 interpreter, 3 needed sonames, 4 version extraction, 5 closed ABI validation, 6 valid. `failure` distinguishes rejection/OS/value/type/key/subprocess/import errors (1–7); `check` is the immutable producer source line. No exception text, host paths, symbol names, or native identities enter this record. The 2GiB per-binary and generic 32MiB captured-tool-output limits remain unchanged. `tool` is 0 generic, 1 symbol scan, 2 relocations, 3 disassembly; `tool_bytes` counts observed stdout bytes, while `tool_exit` and `tool_signal` separately encode nonnegative exit status and terminating signal. A zero exit is required independently of output admission.

Registration verification streams the complete symbol, relocation, and disassembly outputs with a 120-second deadline per tool, at most 64KiB per line, bounded read fragments, and at most 4096 matching relocation slots. It requires exactly one defined registration function symbol and reuses the source-bound direct/GOT call matchers. Even after finding a call it drains output and requires a zero exit. Failure kills the owned tool process group and allows five seconds to reap it. Native addresses and tool diagnostics are never exported. Tests cover a stream larger than 32MiB with less than 2MiB traced Python memory, partial lines, timeout cleanup, exit/signal rejection, duplicate/missing symbols, missing calls, and actual optimized direct/PIC ELF fixtures without application execution.

The exact loader soname `ld-linux-x86-64.so.2` is permitted in DT_NEEDED as well as the program interpreter: ordinary Rust TLS binaries can depend on it directly. The consumer still requires its fixed system loader path and exact version resolution; this does not admit arbitrary loader names or paths. An actual tiny Rust ELF regression exercises this case without executing the application.
